meta.executive_summary: The current deployment of the DIGIT/CMS platform presents critical security vulnerabilities that expose sensitive citizen grievance data to potential compromise. The primary systemic failures stem from a complete lack of defense-in-depth, relying entirely on perimeter cloud security groups while 16 datastore and admin ports are unsafely bound to 0.0.0.0 without an active host firewall. Additionally, unmitigated container escape vectors via Docker socket mounts and insecure remote execution practices during deployment significantly weaken the overall infrastructure posture. Management must immediately prioritize network containment, host-level firewall enforcement, and the removal of privileged container bindings before handling further public-sector traffic.
priority_actions: Immediately reconfigure Docker compose to bind all internal datastores (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, MinIO) and admin UIs to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0.
Enable and configure a host-based firewall (UFW or iptables) on the remote server as a mandatory defense-in-depth layer independent of cloud security groups.
Remove Docker socket mounts from application containers to eliminate immediate container escape and host takeover vectors.
Eliminate remote script piping (curl | sh) from the Ansible deployment path (C: ./deploy.sh) and enforce local script verification with checksum validation.
Re-enable strict SSH host-key verification in the deployment configuration to prevent potential man-in-the-middle attacks during remote server provisioning.

findings.title: CVE-2026-33937 in handlebars 4.7.8 (AST-based RCE)
findings.why: The test-suite lockfile `tests/package-lock.json` resolves the transitive npm dependency `handlebars@4.7.8`, which is affected by published advisory `CVE-2026-33937`. The vulnerable package is introduced through `ts-jest@29.4.6`, and the first fixed release is `4.7.9`.
findings.fix: See the Strix-generated patch for the concrete change.

findings.title: Default fallback API key permits unauthenticated access to privileged kubectl database API
findings.why: The Flask kubectl API authorizes privileged database operations with a shared `X-API-Key` value that falls back to the guessable default `dev-only-key` when `KUBECTL_API_KEY` is unset. Any network-reachable caller who knows that default can invoke sensitive database endpoints without any user or session authentication.
findings.fix: 1. Remove the fallback credential and require `KUBECTL_API_KEY` to be explicitly configured before the Flask service starts. 2. Fail closed when the key is absent, and rotate any environment that may already have exposed or relied on `dev-only-key`. 3. Replace the shared default in notebook and helper code so client tooling never silently sends `dev-only-key`. 4. Treat this API as an administrative interface: restrict network exposure and consider stronger authentication and authorization than a single shared static key.

findings.title: Weak or default credential in deployment config
findings.why: A well-known default credential (e.g. eGov@123, minioadmin, egov123) is baked into the deployment. Unless every call site is overridden, admin/superuser/datastore accounts ship with a guessable password - trivial account takeover, and this repo is PUBLIC.
findings.fix: Remove the hardcoded default: require the value from a vault/secret with no fallback (drop the `default('eGov@123')`), fail the deploy if unset, and rotate any credential that was ever deployed with the default.

findings.title: Datastore or admin port published on all interfaces (0.0.0.0)
findings.why: Publishing the core PostgreSQL database port (5432) directly to all host interfaces (0.0.0.0:15432) exposes the database to the public internet, bypassing the Docker internal network and potential firewall restrictions. An attacker can attempt brute-force attacks or exploit database vulnerabilities directly.
findings.fix:
In docker-compose.egov-digit.yaml under the `postgres-db` service, restrict the port binding to loopback only:
```yaml
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:15432:5432"
```

triage.reason: Postgres and Prometheus ports published on 0.0.0.0 without host firewall protection.

findings.title: Volume Has Sensitive Host Directory
findings.why: Bind-mounting a sensitive host path (`/`, `/etc`, `/var/run`, `/root`) lets the container read or modify host files, breaking isolation between the container and the server.
findings.fix: Mount only the specific sub-directory the service needs, and add `:ro` to make it read-only (e.g. `- ./config:/app/config:ro`). Never mount host system directories.

findings.title: Docker Socket Mounted In Container
findings.why: Mounting the Docker socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`) into the `promtail` container grants root-level control over the Docker daemon on the host. If the promtail container is compromised, an attacker can escape the container, execute arbitrary commands on the host, or take over other containers.
findings.fix:
In docker-compose.egov-digit.yaml under the `promtail` service, remove the Docker socket volume mount:
```yaml
    volumes:
      - ./otel/promtail-config.yaml:/etc/promtail/config.yaml:ro
      - /var/lib/docker/containers:/var/lib/docker/containers:ro
      - promtail_data:/tmp
```

triage.reason: Docker socket mounted read-only into promtail, enabling container escape risks.

findings.title: Remote script piped directly into a shell
findings.why: Piping a remote installation script directly into bash (`curl ... | bash`) executes untrusted code without integrity checking or verification, leaving the host vulnerable to Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks or compromised upstream delivery mechanisms.
findings.fix:
In the Ansible playbook task, download the script to a temporary file, inspect or verify it, and then execute it:
```yaml
    - name: "{{ node_ensure_label }} — install NodeSource Node 20 safely"
      ansible.builtin.shell: |
        set -euo pipefail
        curl -fsSL https://{{ 'deb' if ansible_facts['os_family'] == 'Debian' else 'rpm' }}.nodesource.com/setup_20.x -o /tmp/nodesource_setup.sh
        bash /tmp/nodesource_setup.sh
        {{ 'apt-get' if ansible_facts['os_family'] == 'Debian' else 'dnf' }} install -y nodejs
      args:
        executable: /bin/bash
      when: _node_needs_install | bool
```

triage.reason: Remote install script piped directly into bash shell.

findings.title: Docker image registry used over insecure HTTP
findings.why: Container images are pulled from a registry over plaintext HTTP with TLS verification disabled (insecure-registries). Images run with host-level privileges, so a MITM can substitute a malicious image and take over the host.
findings.fix: Serve the registry over HTTPS with a valid certificate and remove it from `insecure-registries`. If a private CA is used, distribute the CA bundle instead of disabling TLS.

findings.title: SSH host-key verification disabled
findings.why: Disabling SSH host-key checking (`StrictHostKeyChecking=no`) during automated deployment makes the Ansible controller vulnerable to Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks, allowing an attacker to intercept administrative credentials or inject malicious tasks into remote servers.
findings.fix:
In the deployment script (`./deploy.sh`), remove or update the SSH common arguments line:
```bash
        # Remove or change to strict checking:
        ansible_ssh_common_args: '-o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes'
```

triage.reason: SSH host key checking disabled via StrictHostKeyChecking=no.

findings.title: Container Capabilities Unrestricted
findings.why: Containers running with default capabilities retain powerful privileges that can facilitate container escape if an application vulnerability is exploited.
findings.fix:
In docker-compose.egov-digit.yaml, add `cap_drop` to sensitive services:
```yaml
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    cap_add:
      - NET_BIND_SERVICE
```

triage.reason: Container capabilities are not dropped (missing cap_drop: ALL).

findings.title: Security Opt Not Set
findings.why: Without `no-new-privileges`, a process in the container can escalate via setuid binaries; without an seccomp/AppArmor profile it can make syscalls it never needs, enlarging the kernel attack surface.
findings.fix: Add `security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]` to each service (keep the default seccomp profile - do not set `seccomp:unconfined`).

findings.title: Healthcheck Not Set
findings.why: Without a healthcheck the orchestrator cannot tell if the container is actually serving, so failed containers keep receiving traffic.
findings.fix: Add a `healthcheck:` block that probes a real readiness endpoint, e.g. `test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8080/health"]` with sensible `interval`/`retries`.

findings.title: Container Traffic Not Bound To Host Interface
findings.why: Exposing management or proxy ports without binding them to a specific loopback interface makes internal services accessible to anyone with network reachability to the server.
findings.fix:
In docker-compose.egov-digit.yaml, bind ports explicitly to localhost where external access is not required:
```yaml
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:18001:8001"
```

triage.reason: Kong admin and status ports bound to 0.0.0.0 without host firewall protection.

findings.title: Ensure that HTTPS url is used with uri
findings.why: Ansible `uri`/`get_url` tasks that call an http:// endpoint send data (including credentials, tokens and config) over the network in cleartext, exposing it to interception or man-in-the-middle tampering.
findings.fix: Change the task's `url:` from `http://` to `https://`. If the target is an internal service without TLS, front it with a TLS-terminating proxy or document the exception - do not disable certificate validation to work around it.

findings.title: File created without an explicit restrictive mode
findings.why: The file/copy/template task creates a file without an explicit `mode:`, so it inherits the process umask. Config or secret material can land world-readable. The repo's own .ansible-lint suppresses this rule, so its CI never catches it.
findings.fix: Add an explicit least-privilege `mode:` to the task, e.g. `mode: '0640'` for config and `mode: '0600'` for anything holding a secret; `mode: '0750'`/`'0700'` for directories.

findings.title: Ensure that certificate validation isn't disabled with uri
findings.why: Disabling TLS certificate validation lets Ansible trust any certificate, enabling man-in-the-middle interception of the request.
findings.fix: Re-enable certificate validation (`validate_certs: true`) and supply the CA bundle via `ca_path:` if a private CA is in use.

findings.title: Shell pipeline without pipefail (failures go undetected)
findings.why: A shell task pipes commands without `set -o pipefail`, so a failure in any stage except the last is silently ignored - a failed download/verify can still be treated as success (masking supply-chain or deploy errors).
findings.fix: Start the shell with `set -o pipefail` (and add `args: executable: /bin/bash`), or split the pipeline into discrete, checked steps.

findings.title: Privileged Ports Mapped In Container
findings.why: Mapping a privileged host port (below 1024) forces the daemon/container to bind with elevated privileges, widening the attack surface.
findings.fix: Map the service to a high host port (>=1024), e.g. `- "8080:8080"`, and let the reverse proxy terminate 80/443, so containers never bind privileged ports.

findings.title: Host Namespace is Shared
findings.why: Sharing a host namespace (`pid`, `ipc`, or `network`) removes the isolation boundary: the container can see and signal host processes, access host IPC, or bind every host interface.
findings.fix: Remove `pid: host` / `ipc: host` / `network_mode: host` from the service. Use a user-defined bridge network and publish only the ports you need.

findings.title: systemd service runs without hardening (NoNewPrivileges=true)
findings.why: The systemd service runs without sandboxing - typically as root with no NoNewPrivileges/ProtectSystem. If the service (or a payload it runs) is compromised, there is nothing between it and full host control.
findings.fix: Add to the unit's [Service] section: a non-root `User=`, `NoNewPrivileges=true`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, `ProtectHome=true`, `PrivateTmp=true`, and `ReadWritePaths=` limited to what it needs.

findings.title: nginx is missing the security header: server_tokens off
findings.why: The public nginx edge for this citizen-facing government app does not set this security response header, leaving users exposed to protocol downgrade (no HSTS), MIME sniffing (no X-Content-Type-Options), clickjacking, or version disclosure (server_tokens on).
findings.fix: Add the header in the nginx server block: `add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;`, `add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff always;`, `add_header X-Frame-Options DENY always;`, and set `server_tokens off;`.

findings.title: Security lint rule disabled in .ansible-lint
findings.why: The repo's `.ansible-lint` skip/warn list disables a security rule (e.g. risky-file-permissions), so the project's own linting is blind to that class of issue - a governance gap that lets insecure changes pass CI unnoticed.
findings.fix: Remove the security rule from the skip_list (fix the underlying tasks instead), or move it to warn_list only with a documented, time-boxed justification. Keep security rules enforcing in CI.

findings.title: Shared Volumes Between Containers
findings.why: A named/host volume mounted into more than one container lets a compromise in one service read or tamper with another service's data, and can leak secrets written to that volume across trust boundaries.
findings.fix: Give each service its own volume unless sharing is required. Where a volume must be shared, mount it read-only (`:ro`) in every consumer that does not need to write.
